item_name: DUT Racing / Formula Student Team Delft
competition_series: FSG (Formula Student Germany) primary; also FS Italy, FS Netherlands, FSOnline (virtual, COVID-era)
summary: DUT Racing's driverless branch (internally 'FSD'/'Delft Driverless') launched in 2018 by extending the team's existing DUT18 electric race car with sensors, actuators, and software rather than building a bespoke chassis, and did so in formal partnership with MIT Driverless (partnership initiated Summer 2018). The joint 25-person MIT-Delft team reached its first driverless competition within roughly a year, placing 3rd overall in the FSG 2019 Driverless class and 2nd at FS Italy 2019. The program continued through the DUT20D upgrade (2020, new steering actuator, added stereo cameras, relocated compute) and into a COVID-disrupted virtual season (2nd place, FSOnline). DUT Racing also co-created the widely used open-source Formula Student Driverless Simulator (FSDS) with MIT Driverless and FSEast. Public technical documentation is comparatively sparse: strong on 2019 season results and team composition, but weak on EBS actuator design, compute/sensor model numbers, mass, and cost.

ramp_phases: No formally named phases were found in public sources. Informally inferable from the record: (1) platform-selection/partnership phase (2018, choosing DUT18 as the base and forming the MIT partnership), (2) first-build/first-competition phase (2018-2019, reaching FSG 2019 in under a year), (3) upgrade/iteration phase (DUT20D, 2020, targeted component swaps: steering actuator, cameras, compute placement, software robustness), (4) continuation with reduced public documentation (2021-2024, DUT24 referenced but undetailed).

The FSG 2019 Trackdrive result of '9.9 laps completed' (rather than a round number) is a soft signal of an incomplete final lap or a time/lap-count shortfall relative to the full event target, but this is an inference, not a team-stated slip.
platform_prerequisites: Yes - the driverless system was built by extending the existing DUT18 electric race car chassis rather than developing a dedicated driverless chassis, allowing the team to reach its first competition in under about a year from program start.
ebs_design: [uncertain] Team materials mention a 'safety system board' that monitors whether the autonomous system is functioning correctly and 'can deactivate the pneumatic valves' to trigger an emergency stop, implying a pneumatic EBS actuation architecture broadly consistent with DT.3.2, but no source specifies the actuator model, accumulator type/pressure, number of independent circuits, or achieved deceleration.
steering_actuation: [uncertain] DUT20D (2020) is documented as receiving 'a brand new steering actuator,' but no source gives the actuator's motor type, gearing, mounting location, or DT.2.2 decoupling approach. No steering actuator detail was found for the 2019 DUT18-based car.
brake_actuation: [uncertain] not documented separately from the pneumatic EBS system
chassis_impact: The driverless system was integrated onto the existing DUT18 electric chassis (platform reuse rather than a bespoke DV chassis); for DUT20D, relocating the main onboard computer allowed the team to refit the car's original aerodynamics package, implying the initial DV compute placement had disrupted the aero package.
compute_platform: [uncertain] DUT20D (2020) is documented only as having 'the main onboard computer... replaced and moved to a different position' - no model, vendor, or secondary safety MCU is specified in any public source found.
sensor_suite: [uncertain, only generically documented] Team materials describe the driverless system generally as using 'LIDARs and cameras... complex code running on powerful onboard computers,' without model numbers. DUT20D (2020) specifically added 'an extra set of stereo cameras' to the existing suite. No LiDAR model, IMU, GNSS/RTK unit, or wheel-speed/steering-encoder details were found for any DUT Racing car.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: [uncertain] A team-developed 'safety system board' monitors autonomous-system health and can trigger an emergency stop by deactivating pneumatic valves, but its integration into the DT.4 shutdown circuit (DS relay, remote-stop relay, EBS relay) is not documented in detail.
custom_pcbs: A self-developed 'safety system board' for autonomous-system health monitoring and emergency-stop triggering is documented, but its design/fabrication/bring-up duration is not specified.
software_stack: [uncertain, only generically documented] Team materials state the Autonomous department 'develop[s] and integrate[s] sensors, actuators, and software to enable perception, localization, and path planning,' without naming specific frameworks, languages, or middleware. DUT Racing co-developed the open-source Formula Student Driverless Simulator (FSDS) alongside MIT Driverless and FSEast, which includes a ROS2 bridge (fsds_ros2_bridge), suggesting ROS2 familiarity within the broader collaboration, though this is not confirmed as DUT Racing's own onboard middleware.
ros_version: [uncertain] Not confirmed for DUT Racing's own vehicle. The team co-developed FSDS, which ships a ROS2 bridge, but this does not confirm ROS2 use on the physical DUT car.
perception_approach: [uncertain] Only generically described ('LIDARs and cameras' feeding a perception/localization/planning pipeline); no cone-detection algorithm, sensor-fusion method, or achieved detection range is documented for DUT Racing specifically.
slam_localization_approach: [uncertain] Not documented; team materials mention only that the system 'derives the exact position on the race track' without naming a specific SLAM/state-estimation algorithm.
planning_approach: [uncertain] Not documented; described only generically as 'path planning.'
simulation_tooling: DUT Racing co-developed the Formula Student Driverless Simulator (FSDS), an open-source simulator built jointly with MIT Driverless and FSEast (github.com/FS-Driverless/Formula-Student-Driverless-Simulator), which provides a virtual environment with a ROS2 bridge for testing autonomous-system components before track time. Role/extent of FSDS use in DUT Racing's own development process (vs. contribution to the shared tool) is [uncertain].
open_source_repos: github.com/dut-racing - the team's GitHub organization, which per search indexing includes a RoboSense LiDAR SDK for ROS/ROS2 and ROS2 LiDAR packet-messaging packages (useful as a reference for LiDAR driver integration). github.com/FS-Driverless/Formula-Student-Driverless-Simulator (FSDS) - co-developed by DUT Racing, MIT Driverless, and FSEast; a genuinely useful, widely-used open-source reference for any team building a driverless simulation environment.

team_structure_dv: For the 2019 season, the driverless effort was a joint 25-person core team (9 MIT undergraduate/graduate students + 17 TU Delft students, organized across six technical disciplines), with MIT Assistant Professor Luca Carlone as faculty advisor. DUT Racing's overall team (all classes) is 65-85 members per the team's own description; the Autonomous/driverless department is one specialized branch within that, handling sensor integration, localization, and path planning. Exact DV-only headcount for years after 2019 is [uncertain].
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: [uncertain] Not directly documented, though the MIT Driverless partnership itself functioned as an accelerated knowledge-transfer mechanism for the program's first season - this is an inference, not a stated team policy.
budget_estimate: [uncertain] Total/per-year DV budget not disclosed. For the 2019 joint MIT-Delft program, MIT's own reporting names Magna, Waymo, Samsung, and MIT's Edgerton Center as sponsors (largely on the MIT side of the partnership); no comparable DUT Racing-side sponsor or dollar figures were found.
recommended_sequence: Inferred from DUT Racing's own history: (1) select and reuse an existing running EV chassis rather than building a bespoke DV chassis; (2) form an external technical partnership (as with MIT Driverless) to rapidly acquire perception/SLAM/planning expertise rather than developing it purely in-house; (3) target a first competition entry within about a year by scoping to a complete but modest result (3rd place, partial-lap Trackdrive) rather than a podium-winning full stack; (4) in subsequent years, iterate specific subsystems one at a time (as with DUT20D's steering-actuator swap, added stereo cameras, and compute relocation) rather than redesigning the whole stack each season; (5) invest in shared/open-source tooling (as with co-developing FSDS) to reduce simulation development cost.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: DUT Racing's documented pace - forming a partnership and reusing an existing EV chassis to reach a 3rd-place FSG finish in under roughly 12 months - is a strong existence-proof that a first competitive driverless entry is achievable well within a 24-month window when starting from a running EV platform, matching the target team's situation. However, the public record here is thin on exactly which technical choices (EBS design, compute platform, perception algorithm) drove that speed, so DUT Racing is best used as a pacing/organizational-strategy reference (external partnership for expertise, platform reuse, incremental single-subsystem upgrades like DUT20D) rather than a technical-specification source; the target team should pair DUT Racing's timeline benchmark with a team like TUfast (or another team with fuller public specs) for concrete component and software-architecture decisions.
